title: 論語 公冶長第五
source: Confucius 孔子 and his disciples, 論語 (the Analects), book 5, 〈公冶長〉, in the received text as printed in Zhu Xi 朱熹, 論語集注 (part of his 四書章句集注, completed c. 1190), from the Wenyuange 文淵閣 copy of the Siku Quanshu 四庫全書 (1782), as transcribed by the Kanseki Repository (Kanripo, KR1h0015). Collated character by character against two further pre-1930 printings, both transcribed by Kanripo: Ruan Yuan's 1816 Nanchang reprint of the Song edition of 論語注疏 (KR1h0004) and He Yan's 論語集解 in the Sibu Congkan photographic reprint of a Song edition (KR1h0005). Readings that change the sense are noted in the notes; graphic variants (悌 for 弟, 爲 for 為) are not. Zhu Xi's text is substantially the one James Legge printed in The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (Hong Kong, 1861), and the passage numbering is the standard one. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none. Characters are traditional, as the edition prints them (衆, not 眾). Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Any prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same modern Mandarin convention; the exact voice used is recorded in audio/<id>/voice.txt and is fixed for every Chinese text.
about: Book 5 of the Analects, 公冶長 Gōngyě Cháng, named, as every book is, from its first words — the name of a disciple. The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Zhu Xi says this whole book weighs people, ancient and recent, and their worth. It opens with the Master choosing husbands for his daughter and his niece (5.1), and goes on to his verdicts on his own disciples: Zigong a precious vessel (5.3), Zilu's daring outrunning his judgement (5.6), three disciples each fit for office yet not called humane (5.7), Yan Hui able to work out ten things from one (5.8), Zai Yu caught asleep in the daytime (5.9). Then it turns to men of the age before him — statesmen of Lu, Qi, Chu, Wei and Zheng (5.14–5.20) and the ancient worthies Boyi and Shuqi (5.22) — asking of each whether he was humane, a word the Master almost never grants. It closes with the Master and two disciples each stating what they hope for (5.25) and a last saying on the love of learning (5.27). Each numbered passage (5.1–5.27, Zhu Xi's chapters) begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. In two places the edition we follow misprints a character (宰子 for the disciple 宰予 in 5.9, 已 for 己 'oneself' in 5.15); the reading text is corrected and the note says so. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
子謂公冶長：「
可妻也。
雖在縲絏之中，
非其罪也。」
以其子妻之。
sentences.l:
The Master said of Gongye Chang: “He can be given a wife.
Though he was in bonds,
it was not his crime.”
He took his own daughter and gave her to him as wife.
sentences.i: The Master said of Gongye Chang: “He is a man one could marry a daughter to. He has been in prison, but the crime was not his.” And he married his own daughter to him.
sentences.n: The book is named 公冶長 from its first words, the name of a disciple. Zhu Xi: every passage in it weighs men of past and present, worthy or not, right or wrong in what they did — one strand of 'investigating things and exhausting principle'; it has 27 passages, and he records Hu Yin's view that much of it was perhaps written down by Zigong's followers. 公冶長 Gongye Chang (surname Gongye) was a disciple; He Yan's Kong Anguo says he was a man of Lu. 謂 with an object is 'to speak of, say of'. 妻 is read qì here and in the last line, the verb 'to give (a man) a wife' (Zhu Xi: 妻去聲…為之妻也), not qī 'wife'. 縲絏 léi xiè are the black ropes that bound prisoners (Zhu Xi: 縲黑索也，絏攣也), so 'in bonds' is 'in prison'. 以其子妻之 'taking his child, he wived him with her': 以 'taking', 子 'child', here a daughter, 之 'him'. Zhu Xi: nothing can be found out about what kind of man Gongye Chang was, but since the Master called him fit to marry he must have had something to recommend him; and since his time in bonds was not for his own crime, it did him no harm — guilt or innocence lies in oneself, and how can honour or disgrace come from outside?

sentences.t:
子謂南容：「
邦有道，不廢；
邦無道，
免於刑戮。」
以其兄之子妻之。
sentences.l:
The Master said of Nan Rong: “When the state has the Way, he is not left unused;
when the state lacks the Way,
he escapes punishment and execution.”
He took his elder brother's daughter and gave her to him as wife.
sentences.i: The Master said of Nan Rong: “When the state is well governed, he will not be passed over; when it is badly governed, he will escape the headsman.” And he gave him his elder brother's daughter in marriage.
sentences.n: 南容 Nan Rong, Zhu Xi says, was a disciple who lived at Nangong 南宮 (居南宮, usually taken as his surname), personal name Tao 縚 (also given as Kuo 适), courtesy name Zirong 子容, posthumous name Jingshu 敬叔, and elder brother of Meng Yizi of 2.5 — though both the identification with Nangong Jingshu and which brother was the elder are disputed; He Yan's Wang Su calls him Nangong Tao, a man of Lu. 不廢 'not left unused' — Zhu Xi: he would surely be employed; because he was careful in word and deed, he could serve at a well-ruled court and escape harm in a disordered age. He comes back in Book 11. 刑 is punishment, 戮 putting to death. 妻 is qì again, 'to give as wife'. Zhu Xi records a view that Gongye Chang was the lesser man, so the Master gave him his own daughter and Nan Rong his brother's, favouring his brother over himself; he quotes Master Cheng against it: this is peering at the sage with a selfish heart — whoever avoids suspicion is lacking within; the sage is perfectly impartial, and in marrying off a girl one weighs the man to find her match; the ages of the couples and the order of events cannot be known, and to call it avoiding suspicion is quite wrong — a worthy man would not do that, still less a sage.

sentences.t:
子謂子賤：「
君子哉若人！
魯無君子者，
斯焉取斯？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said of Zijian: “A gentleman indeed, this man!
If Lu had no gentlemen,
where would this one have taken this from?”
sentences.i: The Master said of Zijian: “There is a gentleman for you! Yet if Lu had no gentlemen in it, where could he have found the means to become one?”
sentences.n: 子賤 Zijian is Fu Buqi 宓不齊 (宓 is read fú), a disciple; He Yan's Kong Anguo writes the surname 密. 若人 'this man' (He Yan's Bao Xian: 若此人也). 者 at the end of a clause can mark it as a supposition: 魯無君子者 'supposing Lu had no gentlemen'. 焉 is yān, 'where, from what?' (Zhu Xi: 於虔反). The two 斯 are not the same: Zhu Xi takes the first as 'this man' and the second as 'this virtue'. Zhu Xi: Zijian was one who could honour worthy men and choose his friends so as to perfect his own virtue; the Master first sighs at his worth and then asks where he could have got it if Lu had no gentlemen — which shows, too, how many worthies Lu had. He quotes Su (蘇氏): in praising a man's goodness one always traces it to his father and elder brothers, his teachers and friends — the height of generosity.

sentences.t:
子貢問曰：「賜也何如？」
子曰：「女，器也。」
曰：「何器也？」
曰：「瑚璉也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
to be like, to come up to
a hu-lian — a jade-decked grain vessel of the ancestral temple

sentences.l:
Zigong asked, saying: “And Ci — what of him?”
The Master said: “You — a vessel.”
He said: “What vessel?”
He said: “A hu-lian.”
sentences.i: Zigong asked: “And what do you make of me?” The Master said: “You are a vessel.” “What kind of vessel?” “One of the jade-trimmed vessels that hold the grain at the temple offerings.”
sentences.n: 賜 Ci is Zigong's personal name (1.15); speaking of himself by it is the humble form. 女 is rǔ, 'you' (Zhu Xi: 女音汝). 器 is a vessel, a finished thing made for a use (Zhu Xi: 有用之成材) — the 器 of 2.12 'the gentleman is not a vessel', which hangs over the answer. 瑚璉 hú liǎn (Zhu Xi: 璉力展反): vessels that held the millet offered in the ancestral temple — called 瑚 under the Xia, 璉 under the Shang, and 簠簋 under the Zhou — and decked with jade, the most precious and beautiful of vessels. He Yan's Bao Xian gives the same names and calls them the most precious of temple vessels; the Liji ('Mingtang wei') has the two names the other way round, 璉 for the Xia and 瑚 for the Yin. Zhu Xi: Zigong saw that the Master had granted Zijian the name of gentleman, so he asked about himself; the answer means that though he had not reached 'not being a vessel', he was at least a precious one. Variant: He Yan's text reads 賜也如何, the same question in other order.

sentences.t: 或曰：「雍也仁而不佞。」
sentences.l: Someone said: “Yong is humane but not glib.”
sentences.i: Someone said: “Yong is humane, but he has no gift for talk.”
sentences.n: 雍 Yong is Ran Yong 冉雍, courtesy name Zhonggong 仲弓, a disciple (Zhu Xi; He Yan's Ma Rong). 也 after the name sets him up as the topic. 佞 nìng is a ready tongue (Zhu Xi: 口才也) — in the Analects nearly always a fault. 而 here is 'but'. Zhu Xi: Zhonggong was weighty, plain and sparing of words, and the people of the time took a ready tongue for worth, so they praised him for his virtue and regretted that he lacked the talent.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
焉用佞？
禦人以口給，
屢憎於人。
不知其仁，
焉用佞？」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “What use is glibness?
Meeting others with a ready mouth,
one is often hated by others.
I do not know about his humaneness —
but what use is glibness?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “What does he want with a clever tongue? Those who fend people off with quick answers mostly earn their dislike. Whether he is humane I cannot say; but what would he want with a clever tongue?”
sentences.n: 焉 is yān, 'how, what' (Zhu Xi: 於虔反): 焉用佞 'what use glibness?'. 禦 is 'to meet, to answer' (Zhu Xi: 當也，猶應答也); 給 jǐ is 'ready, quick to supply' (Zhu Xi: 辦也); 憎 is 'to hate' (Zhu Xi: 惡也). 於 after a verb can mark the doer: 憎於人 'hated by others'. Zhu Xi: the glib man answers others only with readiness of mouth and no real feeling, and merely gets himself hated; 'though I do not know whether Zhonggong is humane, his not being glib is just what makes him worthy, and no fault' — and saying 'what use glibness?' twice drives it home. Why will the Master not grant him humaneness? Zhu Xi: the Way of humaneness is so great that only one whole in it and unceasing can bear the name; even Yan Hui, next to a sage, could not keep from lapsing after three months (Book 6), so the sage could not lightly grant it to Zhonggong. He Yan's Kong Anguo: 屢 'often'; the glib man's words are quick, and he is often hated by the people. Variant: He Yan's text reads 禦人以給，屢憎民 'answering others with readiness, often hated by the people', and adds 也 after each 焉用佞 and after 不知其仁.

sentences.t:
子使漆雕開仕。
對曰：「吾斯之未能信。」
子説。
sentences.l:
The Master would have Qidiao Kai take office.
He answered, saying: “This — I cannot yet be sure of it.”
The Master was pleased.
sentences.i: The Master wanted Qidiao Kai to take up office. He replied: “Of this I am not yet confident.” The Master was pleased.
sentences.n: 漆雕開 Qidiao Kai was a disciple, courtesy name Ziruo 子若 (Zhu Xi); He Yan's Kong Anguo: Qidiao the surname, Kai the name. 使…仕 'to have him take office'. 吾斯之未能信 puts the object first: 斯 'this' stands before the verb, marked by 之, the pattern of 2.6 唯其疾之憂. 説 is the edition's form of 說, read yuè, 'pleased' (Zhu Xi: 説音悦). Zhu Xi: 斯 points to the principle of the thing — what one must know to govern others; 信 is truly knowing it to be so without a hair's breadth of doubt; Kai said he could not yet, so could not yet govern men, and the Master was pleased at how earnest his will was. He quotes Master Cheng: Kai had already seen the main idea, so the Master was pleased; and Xie Liangzuo: nothing is known of Kai's learning, but if the sage sent him into office his talent must have fitted him for it; in the subtle workings of the heart, a single hair not yet his own meant he was not yet sure — this the sage could not know and Kai knew for himself; his talent was enough for office, but his measure would not rest in small attainment. He Yan's Zheng Xuan: the Master was glad that his will was so deeply set on the Way.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
道不行，
乘桴浮于海。
從我者，其由與？」
子路聞之喜。
子曰：「
由也好勇過我，
無所取材。」

morph.gloss: measure (= 裁 cái, 'to cut to fit')

sentences.l:
The Master said: “The Way does not go forward —
I will ride a raft and drift out on the sea.
The one to follow me — would it be Yóu?”
Zilu heard it and was glad.
The Master said: “Yóu loves courage beyond me,
but has nothing to take his measure by.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The Way is getting nowhere. I shall take a raft and let the sea carry me — and if anyone comes with me, it will surely be Yóu.” Zilu heard this and was delighted. The Master said: “Yóu's love of daring outruns mine; but he has no means of weighing things up.”
sentences.n: 由 Yóu is Zhong You 仲由, courtesy name Zilu 子路 (2.17). 乘 here is chéng, 'to ride, to board' (not shèng 'chariot'); 桴 fú is a raft (Zhu Xi: 筏也; He Yan's Ma Rong: bamboo or wood lashed together, the big ones called 筏 and the small 桴). 于 = 於. 從 Zhu Xi reads zòng, 'to follow in attendance' (從…去聲), a reading modern practice does not keep; we give cóng. 其…與 'would it be…?': 其 softens, and 與 is the question particle yú (Zhu Xi: 平聲). 好 is hào 'to love' (Zhu Xi: 去聲). The last word is the puzzle. Zhu Xi: 材 here is 裁 'to cut, to judge', the old graph borrowed (材與裁同，古字借用). He quotes Master Cheng: the sigh about the sea grieves that the world has no worthy ruler; Zilu was brave for what is right, so the Master said he would follow — all said in supposition; Zilu took it as real and was glad to be chosen, so the Master praised his courage and mocked his inability to weigh the principle of things and fit it to what is right. He Yan's Zheng Xuan reads it as a joke: Zilu missed the hidden meaning, so the Master teased him — 'there is nowhere to get timber for the raft'. Variant: He Yan's text reads 浮於海 and 其由也與.

sentences.t:
孟武伯問：「子路仁乎？」
子曰：「不知也。」

morph.gloss: Meng, the clan name (Mengsun, Zhongsun) of Lu
Wu, posthumous name of Meng Wubo
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Meng Wubo asked: “Is Zilu humane?”
The Master said: “I do not know.”
sentences.i: Meng Wubo asked whether Zilu was humane. The Master said: “I cannot say.”
sentences.n: 孟武伯 Meng Wubo is the Zhongsun Zhi of 2.6, head of the Meng house of Lu. Zhu Xi: as for humaneness, Zilu was among those who 'reach it for a day or a month' (Book 6) — now there, now gone — so the Master could not be sure whether he had it or not, and answered that he did not know. He Yan's Kong Anguo: the Way of humaneness is so great that it cannot be granted to anyone entire.

sentences.t:
又問。
子曰：「由也，
千乗之國，
可使治其賦也；
不知其仁也。」

morph.gloss: war chariot (乗, the edition's form of 乘)
levies — the army raised from the fields

sentences.l:
He asked again.
The Master said: “Yóu —
a state of a thousand chariots:
he could be set to manage its levies.
I do not know about his humaneness.”
sentences.i: He asked again. The Master said: “Yóu could be put in charge of the levies of a state of a thousand chariots. Whether he is humane I cannot say.”
sentences.n: 千乗 is the edition's form of 千乘 (1.5), 'a thousand chariots', the measure of a major state; 乗 is the same word, read shèng (Zhu Xi: 乘去聲). 由也 'as for Yóu': 也 after a name sets up the topic. 可使 'could be made to, could be employed to'. 賦 is a levy. Zhu Xi: here it means troops — in old times the army was raised by levy on the fields, so troops were called 賦, as in the Zuo zhuan's 悉索敝賦 'gather all our poor levies'; He Yan's Kong Anguo: the military levy. Zhu Xi: this is what can be seen of Zilu's talent; his humaneness cannot be known.

sentences.t:
求也何如？
子曰：「求也，
千室之邑，
百乘之家，
可使為之宰也；
不知其仁也。」

morph.gloss: to be like, to come up to

sentences.l:
“Qiu — what of him?”
The Master said: “Qiu —
a town of a thousand households,
a house of a hundred chariots:
he could be set to act as its steward.
I do not know about his humaneness.”
sentences.i: “And Qiu?” The Master said: “Qiu could be made steward of a town of a thousand households, or of a house that musters a hundred chariots. Whether he is humane I cannot say.”
sentences.n: 求 Qiu is Ran Qiu 冉求, courtesy name Ziyou 子有 — the 冉有 of 3.6, who served the Ji house. 千室之邑 'a town of a thousand households', which Zhu Xi calls a large town; 百乘之家 'a house of a hundred chariots' is the household of a minister or grandee (Zhu Xi: 卿大夫之家; He Yan's Kong Anguo: a feudal lord has a thousand chariots, a minister or grandee a hundred). 乘 is shèng. 為之宰 'act as its steward': 為 is wéi, and 之 'its' covers both the town and the house. 宰, Zhu Xi says, is the common title of a town's head and of a great house's chief retainer.

sentences.t:
赤也何如？
子曰：「赤也，
束帶立於朝，
可使與賔客言也；
不知其仁也。」

morph.gloss: to be like, to come up to
guests (賔, the edition's form of 賓)

sentences.l:
“Chi — what of him?”
The Master said: “Chi —
sash bound on, standing at court,
he could be set to speak with guests and visitors.
I do not know about his humaneness.”
sentences.i: “And Chi?” The Master said: “Chi, in his court sash, standing in the hall, could be given the task of receiving envoys and guests. Whether he is humane I cannot say.”
sentences.n: 赤 Chi is Gongxi Chi 公西赤, courtesy name Zihua 子華, a disciple (Zhu Xi; He Yan's Ma Rong). 束帶 'binding on the sash', in full court dress. 朝 is cháo, 'court' (Zhu Xi: 音潮), not zhāo 'morning'. 賔 is the edition's form of 賓 bīn; 賓客 are guests and visitors, here envoys from other states. 與 is yǔ, 'with'. Ma Rong: Chi had a fine bearing and could serve as the officer who receives envoys. The three answers have one shape: a talent the Master can vouch for, and humaneness he will not.

sentences.t: 子謂子貢曰：「女與回也，孰愈？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l: The Master said to Zigong: “You and Hui — which is the better?”
sentences.i: The Master said to Zigong: “Set yourself beside Hui: which of you comes out ahead?”
sentences.n: 謂…曰 here is 'spoke to … saying', not 'said of' as in 5.1–5.2. 女 is rǔ, 'you' (Zhu Xi: 女音汝，下同 'and so below'); 與 is yǔ, 'and'. 回 Hui is Yan Hui 顏回 (2.9), the disciple the Master loved most. 孰 shú 'which (of the two)'; 愈 yù 'to surpass, be better' (Zhu Xi and He Yan's Kong Anguo: 勝也).

sentences.t:
對曰：「賜也何敢望回？
回也聞一以知十；
賜也聞一以知二。」
sentences.i: He answered: “How could I so much as set my sights on Hui? Hui learns one thing and from it works out ten; I learn one and get to two.”
sentences.n: Zigong calls himself by his personal name 賜, as is proper before his teacher. 望 is to gaze at from afar — to aspire to, hope to come level with. 以 joins the two verbs: 'hear one, and by it know ten'. Zhu Xi: one is the beginning of numbers and ten their end; two is one's counterpart. Yan Hui's clear and penetrating mind saw the end in the beginning; Zigong worked things out by inference, getting from this to that. The proofs, he says, are Hui's 'nothing in my words he does not delight in' (Book 11) and Zigong's 'told what has gone, he knows what is to come' (1.15).

sentences.t:
子曰：「弗如也！
吾與女弗如也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Not equal to him!
I agree with you: not equal.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “No, you are not his equal. You are right — you are not.”
sentences.n: 弗 fú is 'not', a negative that usually leaves its object understood: 弗如 'not equal (him)'. 女 is rǔ, 'you'. 與 here Zhu Xi glosses 許 'to grant, to agree with' (read yǔ): 'I grant you that you are not his equal'. He Yan's Bao Xian reads it as 'and': 'I and you are both not his equal' — the Master consoling Zigong. Zhu Xi quotes Hu Yin: Zigong was given to comparing people (Book 14), and the Master, having told him he himself had no leisure for that, now asked how he stood beside Hui, to see how well he knew himself. To hear one and know ten is the gift of the highest wisdom, next to those born knowing; to hear one and know two is the talent of a man above the middle, who learns and then knows. Zigong had long measured himself against Hui and seen he could not reach him; the Master approved his clear self-knowledge and his ease in bowing to another, so he agreed with him and granted it again — and this is why Zigong came in the end to hear about human nature and the Way of Heaven (5.12).

sentences.t:
宰予晝寢。
子曰：「
朽木不可雕也，
糞土之牆不可杇也；
於予與何誅？」

morph.gloss: Zai Yu — the disciple Zai Wo

sentences.l:
Zai Yu slept in the daytime.
The Master said: “Decayed wood cannot take carving;
a wall of dung and earth cannot take plaster.
As for Yu — what blame?”
sentences.i: Zai Yu was asleep in the daytime. The Master said: “You can carve nothing out of timber that has gone soft, and you cannot put a smooth coat on a wall of muck. Yu is not worth the scolding.”
sentences.n: The print has 宰子, a misprint for 宰予, corrected here. (Both collation witnesses read 宰予, Zhu Xi's own comment says 宰予, and the Master goes on to call him 予; the Siku copy's 子 recurs in a Hu Yin quotation in Zhu Xi's comment on the next unit.) 宰予 Zai Yu, courtesy name Ziwo 子我, is the Zai Wo 宰我 of 3.21, known for his ready tongue. 晝寢 Zhu Xi: sleeping when it is broad day. 朽 xiǔ is 'rotten' (Zhu Xi: 腐也); 雕 is 'to carve and engrave' (Zhu Xi: 刻畫也); 杇 wū (Zhu Xi: 音汚) is a plasterer's trowel, here the verb 'to plaster' (Zhu Xi: 鏝也). After 不可 the verb is passive in sense: 不可雕 'cannot be carved'. 於予與 'toward Yu': 予 is Zai Yu's personal name, read yǔ, not the pronoun yú 'I'; 與 is yú (Zhu Xi: 平聲), a pausing particle (語辭). 誅 'to blame, to rebuke' (Zhu Xi: 責也). Zhu Xi: his will and spirit were dull and slack, so teaching had nothing to take hold of; saying he is not worth blaming is the deepest blame. He Yan's Kong Anguo reads it the same: 'what blame shall I lay on you?' — the words of deep reproof. Variant: He Yan's text writes 彫 for 雕.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
始吾於人也，
聽其言而信其行；
今吾於人也，
聽其言而觀其行。
於予與改是。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “At first, toward others,
I heard their words and trusted their conduct;
now, toward others,
I hear their words and watch their conduct.
With Yu I changed this.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “There was a time when, hearing what a man said, I believed he would act on it. Now, hearing what he says, I watch what he does. Yu changed that in me.”
sentences.n: A second 子曰 inside one passage is odd, and Zhu Xi quotes Hu Yin: 'the 子曰 is perhaps an intrusion; otherwise this was said on another day'. 於人也 'in my dealings with people'. 行 is conduct; Zhu Xi reads this noun xìng (行去聲), a reading modern practice does not keep, and we give xíng. 予 is yǔ and 與 yú, as in the line before. 改是 'changed this'. Zhu Xi: Zai Yu could talk, but his conduct did not come up to his words, so the Master says that it was over Yu that he corrected this mistake — a further warning to him. He quotes Fan Zuyu: the gentleman in learning works at it day after day and stops only at death, afraid only of falling short; Zai Yu sleeping by day — what self-abandonment could be worse? And Hu Yin again: Zai Yu could not command his energy with his will; lying down when tired is the energy of ease winning over the will to keep watch; the sages never failed to fear sloth, which is why Confucius blamed him so deeply; the sage did not need this to learn to watch conduct, nor did it make him doubt all his pupils — he used it to teach them to be careful in speech and quick in deed. He Yan's Kong Anguo: the change came from Zai Wo's sleeping by day.

sentences.t:
子曰：「吾未見剛者。」
或對曰：「申棖。」
子曰：「棖也慾，
焉得剛？」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “I have not yet seen one who is firm.”
Someone answered, saying: “Shen Cheng.”
The Master said: “Cheng has desires —
how can he be firm?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “I have never met a man of real firmness.” Someone answered: “There is Shen Cheng.” The Master said: “Cheng has too many cravings — how could he be firm?”
sentences.n: 剛 gāng is hard and strong, not to be bent (Zhu Xi: 堅強不屈之意) — the thing men find hardest of all, so the Master sighs that he has not seen it. 申棖 Shen Cheng was a disciple (Zhu Xi; He Yan's Bao Xian: a man of Lu). 棖也慾 has no verb 'to be': the noun 慾 'desire' serves as the predicate — Zhu Xi: 'many cravings' (多嗜慾); He Yan's Kong Anguo: 'many passions and desires'. 焉 is yān, 'how?'. Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: a man with desires is not firm; the firm are not bent by desire. And Xie Liangzuo: firmness and desire are exact opposites — to master things is firmness, and so one stands above them; to be smothered by things is desire, and so one bows beneath them; those with a true will have always been few, so it is no wonder the Master had not seen it; what Shen Cheng desired cannot be known, but he was perhaps a stiff man pleased with himself, whom some took for firm, not seeing that this was just what made it desire.

sentences.t:
子貢曰：「
我不欲人之加諸我也，
吾亦欲無加諸人。」
子曰：「賜也，
非爾所及也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
(makes 'others lay it on me' a noun phrase)

sentences.l:
Zigong said: “What I do not want others to lay upon me,
I too want not to lay upon others.”
The Master said: “Ci,
this is not what you have reached.”
sentences.i: Zigong said: “Whatever I would not have others put upon me, I want to keep from putting upon them.” The Master said: “Ci, you are not there yet.”
sentences.n: 諸 is the fused 之於 'it upon'. 之 between 人 and 加 turns 人之加諸我 into one noun phrase, 'others' laying (it) upon me' (the 1.16 pattern). 無 negates the wish: 欲無加 'want not to lay'. 爾所及 'what you reach': 所 makes the verb a noun, with 爾 'you' as its subject. Zhu Xi: what I do not want others to do to me I also do not want to do to others — this is the humane man's affair, done without forcing, and so not within Zigong's reach. He quotes Master Cheng: this is humaneness; 'what you would not have done to yourself, do not do to others' (the Doctrine of the Mean's 施諸己而不願，亦勿施於人) is fellow-feeling; fellow-feeling Zigong might reach by effort, humaneness not. Zhu Xi adds in his own voice: 無 'not' is what comes of itself, 勿 'do not' is a prohibition — that is the difference between humaneness and fellow-feeling. He Yan's Ma Rong glosses 加 as 陵 'to encroach on'; his Kong Anguo takes the reply as 'you cannot stop others from wronging you'. Variant: He Yan's text adds 也 after 加諸人.

sentences.t:
子貢曰：「
夫子之文章，
可得而聞也；
夫子之言性與天道，
不可得而聞也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
outward pattern — his bearing and words
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zigong said: “The Master's outward pattern —
that one may come to hear;
the Master's speaking on human nature and the Way of Heaven —
that one may not come to hear.”
sentences.i: Zigong said: “What shows of the Master's learning — his bearing, his words — is there for all of us to take in. But what he has to say about our nature and about the Way of Heaven, we are not given to hear.”
sentences.n: 文章 is the outward pattern of a man's cultivation. Zhu Xi: virtue as it shows itself outside — a dignified bearing and graceful words are all of it; He Yan's comment: 章 is 'bright', the pattern and substance plain to see, which ear and eye can take in. 性 xìng is human nature, which Zhu Xi calls the principle of Heaven as man receives it; 天道 'the Way of Heaven' is that principle as it is in itself — at bottom, he says, one principle. 可得而聞 'can manage to hear': 得 'to manage, to get to', 而 leading on to the second verb. Zhu Xi: the Master's pattern showed every day, and all his learners heard it; of human nature and the Way of Heaven he seldom spoke, and some learners never heard, for in the sage's school teaching did not skip steps — Zigong now heard it for the first time and sighed at its beauty. He quotes Master Cheng: these are Zigong's words of praise on hearing the Master's highest teaching. He Yan's comment: human nature is what man is born with; the Way of Heaven is the Way of origination and success renewed daily; being deep and subtle, it cannot be heard. Variant: He Yan's text ends 不可得而聞也已矣, '…cannot be heard, and that is all'.

sentences.t:
子路有聞，
未之能行，
唯恐有聞。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zilu, having heard something
and not yet able to practise it,
feared only to hear more.
sentences.i: When Zilu had been taught something and had not yet managed to put it into practice, his one fear was that he would be taught something more.
sentences.n: 有聞 'to have something heard', to be taught a thing. 未之能行 'not yet it could practise': after the negative 未, the pronoun object 之 comes forward, here before the auxiliary 能. 唯 wéi 'only'. Zhu Xi: what he had heard before he had not yet carried out, so he feared hearing more and not having the means to act on it all. He quotes Fan Zuyu: Zilu, hearing what was good, was bold to carry it out at once; the disciples felt they could not match him, so they wrote it down — Zilu can be called a man who knew how to use his courage. He Yan's Kong Anguo reads it the same. Variant: He Yan's text reads 未能行, without 之.

sentences.t:
子貢問曰：「
孔文子何以謂之文也？」
子曰：「
敏而好學，
不恥下問，
是以謂之文也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
Kong Wenzi — Kong Yu, a grandee of Wei

sentences.l:
Zigong asked, saying: “Kong Wenzi — by what is he called Wen?”
The Master said: “Quick, and fond of learning;
not ashamed to ask below:
by this he is called Wen.”
sentences.i: Zigong asked: “Why was Kong Wenzi given the name Wen, ‘the Cultured’?” The Master said: “He was quick, and he loved learning, and he was not ashamed to put questions to men beneath him. That is why he was called Wen.”
sentences.n: 孔文子 Kong Wenzi is Kong Yu 孔圉, a grandee of Wei 衞 (Zhu Xi; He Yan's Kong Anguo); 文 Wen, 'cultured', was his posthumous title. 何以 'by what', the question word coming before 以 (as in 2.7); 是以 'by this', the same order. 謂之文 'call him Wen', with no subject stated: people in general. 不恥下問 'not ashamed to ask downward', to put questions to those below him. 好 is hào (Zhu Xi: 去聲). Zhu Xi: men quick by nature are mostly not fond of learning, and men of high rank are mostly ashamed to ask those below; so the rules for posthumous titles count 'diligent in learning and fond of asking' as Wen — a hard thing for anyone — and Kong Yu got Wen for this. He quotes Su (蘇氏): Kong Wenzi made Taishu Ji send away his wife and married him to his own daughter; Ji carried on with his first wife's younger sister; Wenzi in anger meant to attack him and consulted Confucius, who gave no answer, called for his carriage and left; Ji fled to Song, and Wenzi gave his daughter to Ji's younger brother. Such was the man who was named Wen — hence Zigong's doubt; Confucius would not bury his good points, and doing this much was enough for Wen, though not the Wen 'that warps Heaven and wefts Earth'. Kong Anguo: 敏 is quickness of understanding.

sentences.t:
子謂子産：「
有君子之道四焉：
其行己也恭，
其事上也敬，
其養民也惠，
其使民也義。」

morph.gloss: Zichan — Gongsun Qiao, minister of Zheng
Chan (his courtesy name; 産 = 產)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: The Master said of Zichan: “There were four marks of the gentleman in him. He bore himself with modesty, served those above him with reverence, looked after the people with kindness, and set them to work as was right.”
sentences.n: The print has 已, a misprint for 己, corrected here. (其行己 'his conducting of himself' needs 己 'oneself'; our first collation witness reads 己, and He Yan's text prints 巳, its form for both — the same confusion as at 4.14.) 子産 Zichan (産 is the edition's form of 產 chǎn) is Gongsun Qiao 公孫僑, the great minister of Zheng 鄭 and an older contemporary of Confucius (Zhu Xi; He Yan's Kong Anguo). 焉 is 'in him'. Four lines of one shape: 其 + verb phrase, 也 to pause, then the quality — 'his serving superiors, (it was) reverent'. Zhu Xi: 恭 is modest and yielding, 敬 careful and attentive, 惠 loving and doing good; employing the people rightly is such as (in the Zuo zhuan) his giving town and country their rules, high and low their proper dress, fields their boundaries and ditches, and houses and wells their groups of five. 養 is yǎng. Zhu Xi quotes a Mr Wu (吳氏): to list a man's faults and blame him means most of what he did was good — as with Zang Wenzhong's 'three things inhumane, three unwise' in the Zuo zhuan; to list his good points and praise them means something was still lacking — as here; to sum a man up in a phrase, or an age in one event, is wrong either way.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
晏平仲善與人交，
久而敬之。」

morph.gloss: Yan Pingzhong — Yan Ying, minister of Qi

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Yan Pingzhong was good at dealing with others:
long acquainted, and still he respected them.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Yan Pingzhong knew how to keep a friendship: however long he had known a man, his respect for him never wore thin.”
sentences.n: 晏平仲 Yan Pingzhong is Yan Ying 晏嬰, grandee and minister of Qi 齊 and an older contemporary of Confucius (Zhu Xi; He Yan's Zhou Shenglie, who adds that 平 Ping was his posthumous title). 善 + verb is 'good at': 善與人交 'good at dealing with others'; 與 is yǔ, 'with'. 久而 'long, and yet'. Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: as acquaintance grows long, respect fades; to keep respecting a man after long acquaintance — that is what makes him good at it. Variant: He Yan's text reads 久而人敬之, 'long acquainted, and others respected him' — the praise is then for the respect he went on receiving from others, not the respect he kept for them.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
臧文仲居蔡，
山節，
藻棁，
何如其知也？」

morph.gloss: Zang Wenzhong — Zangsun Chen, grandee of Lu
to be like, to come up to

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Zang Wenzhong housed a great tortoise,
hills on the capitals,
waterweed on the king-posts —
what kind of wisdom is his?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Zang Wenzhong kept a great tortoise in a chamber with mountains carved on the bracket-blocks and waterweed painted on the roof-posts. What sort of wisdom is that?”
sentences.n: 臧文仲 Zang Wenzhong was a grandee of Lu of the Zangsun house, personal name Chen 辰 (Zhu Xi; He Yan's Bao Xian), who died some decades before Confucius was born. 居 Zhu Xi glosses as 藏 'to keep, to store'. 蔡 is a great tortoise, kept for divination; Bao Xian says it was named from the land of Cai where it came from, was a foot and two inches long, and was a ruler's tortoise — so keeping it was itself a usurpation. 節 are the bracket-blocks on top of the pillars; 藻 is a waterweed; 棁 zhuō (Zhu Xi: 章悦反) are the short posts that stand on the beams. 知 is zhì, 'wisdom' (Zhu Xi: 去聲). 何如其知也 'what kind of thing is his wisdom?'. Zhu Xi: he built a house for the tortoise with hills carved on the blocks and weed painted on the posts; people of the time thought him wise, but the Master says he neglected what is right toward the people and fawned on and profaned the spirits — how could that count as wise? The Zuo zhuan's 'made empty vessels' refers to this. He quotes Zhang Zai: the decorated tortoise-house and the sacrifice to the sea-bird Yuanju 爰居 come together in their unwisdom. Bao Xian reads the carving and painting as extravagance.

sentences.t:
子張問曰：「令尹子文三仕為令尹，無喜色；
三已之，無慍色。
舊令尹之政，
必以告新令尹。
何如？」
子曰：「忠矣。」
曰：「仁矣乎？」
曰：「未知，
焉得仁？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
to be like, to come up to

sentences.l:
Zizhang asked, saying: “The Chief Minister Ziwen three times took office as Chief Minister and had no glad look;
three times was dismissed and had no resentful look.
The old Chief Minister's government
he always made known to the new Chief Minister.
What of him?”
The Master said: “Wholehearted.”
He said: “Humane?”
He said: “I do not know —
how would he be humane?”
sentences.i: Zizhang asked: “Ziwen, Chief Minister of Chu, was three times appointed to the office and never looked pleased; three times he was put out of it and never looked aggrieved. And each time he made sure to tell the new Chief Minister how things had been run. What do you say of him?” The Master said: “He was wholehearted.” “Was he humane?” “I cannot say. How would that make him humane?”
sentences.n: 子張 Zizhang is Zhuansun Shi (2.18). 令尹 is the title of the chief minister of Chu 楚, the highest office of that state (Zhu Xi: 楚上卿執政者). 子文 Ziwen was of the Dou 鬭 clan, personal name Gouwutu 穀於菟 (Zhu Xi; He Yan's Kong Anguo). 三已之 'three times (they) dismissed him': 已 'to stop' used of a person, 'to remove from office'. 以告 'took (it) and told', 以 with its object left out. 何如 'what of him?'. Zhu Xi: he showed neither joy nor anger, set no gap between others and himself, knew there was his state and not that there was himself — great wholeheartedness, which is why Zizhang suspected he was humane; but it is not known that his three appointments, three dismissals and briefing of his successor all came from heavenly principle with no selfish desire in them, so the Master granted him wholeheartedness and not humaneness. 知 here is zhī, 'to know' (Zhu Xi: 知如字 'in its ordinary reading'), and 焉 yān 'how'; the note sets aside the other possible reading, 知 as zhì, 'he was not yet wise — how could he be humane?'. Kong Anguo: 'I have only heard of his wholehearted acts; I do not know about his humaneness.' Variant: He Yan's text reads 舊令尹之攻 (攻 'attack', a copyist's slip for 政) and 何如也.

sentences.t:
崔子弑齊君，
陳文子有馬十乘，棄而違之。
至於他邦，
則曰：「猶吾大夫崔子也。」
違之。
之一邦，
則又曰：「猶吾大夫崔子也。」
違之。
何如？
子曰：「清矣。」
曰：「仁矣乎？」
曰：「未知，
焉得仁？」

morph.gloss: Cuizi — Cui Zhu, grandee of Qi
Chen Wenzi — Chen Xuwu, grandee of Qi
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
to be like, to come up to

sentences.l:
“Cuizi assassinated the lord of Qi.
Chen Wenzi had ten teams of horses; he abandoned them and left it.
Coming to another state,
he said: ‘They are like our grandee Cuizi,’
and left it.
Going on to one more state,
he said again: ‘They are like our grandee Cuizi,’
and left it.
What of him?”
The Master said: “Pure.”
He said: “Humane?”
He said: “I do not know —
how would he be humane?”
sentences.i: “When Cuizi murdered the lord of Qi, Chen Wenzi, who had forty horses, left them behind and quit the state. In the next state he came to, he said, ‘They are no better than our own grandee Cuizi,’ and moved on. In the one after that he said the same thing again, and moved on. What do you say of him?” The Master said: “He was pure.” “Was he humane?” “I cannot say. How would that make him humane?”
sentences.n: Zizhang goes on to a second case; the Chinese leaves his speech unmarked here. 崔子 Cuizi is Cui Zhu 崔杼, a grandee of Qi; 齊君 'the lord of Qi' is Duke Zhuang 莊公, personal name Guang 光 (Zhu Xi), killed in 548 BC. 弑 shì is the word for a subject killing his lord or a son his father. 陳文子 Chen Wenzi was another grandee of Qi, personal name Xuwu 須無. 乘 is shèng, a team of four horses, so ten teams are forty horses (Zhu Xi: 十乘四十匹也). 違 'to leave' (Zhu Xi: 去也). In 違之。之一邦 the first 之 is 'it' and the second is the verb 'to go to'. 猶 'is like'. Zhu Xi: Wenzi kept himself clean and left the disorder — that can be called pure; but it is not known whether his heart truly saw that this was right and shook himself free of every tie, or whether he could not help himself out of private concern for gain and harm and was still not free of resentment and regret; so the Master granted him purity, not humaneness. Zhu Xi then gives what he heard from his teacher (Li Tong): to accord with principle without a selfish heart is humaneness; neither man showed for certain that he did; Zizhang, not yet knowing what humaneness is, admired what is hard to do and took small things as proof of great ones. The comment then adds, from other books, that Ziwen's plans for Chu were all for usurping the royal title and harrying the Chinese states, and that Wenzi failed to set his lord right or punish the murderer, and within a few years went back to Qi. 知 is zhī, as above. Variant: He Yan's text has 則又曰 at the first stop too, and 違之至一邦 'left it and came to a state' for 違之之一邦.

sentences.t:
季文子三思而後行。
子聞之，曰：「再，斯可矣。」

morph.gloss: Ji Wenzi — Jisun Xingfu, grandee of Lu

sentences.l:
Ji Wenzi thought three times and only then acted.
The Master heard of it and said: “Twice — that would serve.”
sentences.i: Ji Wenzi would turn a thing over in his mind three times before he acted on it. When the Master heard this he said: “Twice over would be plenty.”
sentences.n: 季文子 Ji Wenzi is Jisun Xingfu 季孫行父, a grandee of Lu (Zhu Xi; He Yan's Zheng Xuan) who died before Confucius was born, so the Master 'heard of' him from others. 三 is sān; Zhu Xi reads it sàn (三去聲), 'three times over', a reading modern practice does not keep. 而後 'and after that' — 'only then'. 斯 'then', which Zhu Xi calls a particle (語辭). Zhu Xi: he thought three times before every act — as when, sent on a mission to Jin, he first looked up the rites for meeting a death on the road. He quotes Master Cheng: a man who does evil never thinks; once he thinks, he does good; but twice is already careful enough, and at three times selfish notions arise and he is confused instead — so the Master mocked him. Zhu Xi adds in his own voice: Wenzi weighed things so carefully that he should have made no false step; yet when Duke Xuan usurped the throne he could not punish it, and instead went to Qi as his envoy to pay bribes — proof of 'selfish notions arise'; so the gentleman works at exhausting principle and prizes decision, and does not value much thinking for its own sake. Zheng Xuan reads it as praise: Wenzi was wholehearted and worthy, made few mistakes, and had no need to go as far as three times. Variant: He Yan's text reads 再思斯可矣, 'thinking twice — then it will do'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「甯武子：
邦有道則知；
邦無道則愚。
其知可及也；
其愚不可及也。」

morph.gloss: Ning Wuzi — Ning Yu, grandee of Wei

sentences.i: The Master said: “When the state was well governed, Ning Wuzi was a wise man; when it went astray, he was a fool. Others could rise to his wisdom; none could rise to his folly.”
sentences.n: 甯武子 Ning Wuzi is Ning Yu 甯俞, a grandee of Wei 衞 (Zhu Xi; He Yan's Ma Rong, who adds that 武 Wu was his posthumous title). 知 is zhì, 'wise, wisdom', both times (Zhu Xi: 知去聲). 則 'then'. 可及 'can be reached, can be come up to'. Zhu Xi, from the Zuo zhuan: Wuzi served Wei under Duke Wen and Duke Cheng; Duke Wen had the Way and Wuzi did nothing to be seen — that is wisdom others can reach; Duke Cheng lacked the Way and lost his state, and Wuzi went about in the thick of it, giving all his heart and strength and not shunning hardship or danger — doing just what every clever man would shun — and yet in the end kept himself safe and saved his lord: that is foolishness no one can reach. He quotes Master Cheng: when the state lacks the Way, to hide one's light and escape harm is what cannot be reached; though there are men who ought not to play the fool, such as Bi Gan 比干, who died remonstrating with the last Shang king. So Zhu Xi's 'foolishness' is loyal service no prudent man would take on; He Yan's Kong Anguo reads it as feigned stupidity, 'so like the real thing that no one could match it'.

sentences.t:
子在陳，曰：「歸與！歸與！
吾黨之小子狂簡，
斐然成章，
不知所以裁之。」
sentences.l:
The Master, in Chen, said: “Go back! Go back!
The young men of my circle are wild and slight;
brightly patterned, they make up a finished design,
and do not know how to cut it.”
sentences.i: When the Master was in Chen he said: “Time to go back! Time to go back! The young men of my following at home aim high and pay little heed to detail; they have woven something bright and complete, and do not know how to trim it to shape.”
sentences.n: 陳 Chen was a small state to the south-west of Lu, where the Master stayed for some years on his travels. Zhu Xi: these are the words of the Master, after wandering through the states without his Way being put into practice, longing to go home. 與 is yú (Zhu Xi: 平聲), an exclamation. 吾黨之小子 'the young men of my circle' — Zhu Xi: the disciples who were in Lu. 狂簡 Zhu Xi: large in aim and careless of detail; He Yan's Kong Anguo takes 簡 as 'great': they reached boldly for the great Way. 斐 fěi (Zhu Xi: 音匪) is the look of pattern; 然 after a descriptive word makes 'in such a way': 斐然 'patterned-like, bright'. 成章 Zhu Xi: the pattern of their learning has come to something worth looking at. 裁 'to cut and correct' (Zhu Xi: 割正也); 所以裁之 'that by which to cut it'. Zhu Xi: the Master had first hoped to practise his Way in the world; now he knew he would never be used, so he turned to forming those who came after, to hand on the Way to later ages; not finding men who walk the middle path, he thought of the next best — the wild, whose aims are high and who might still go forward in the Way — and only feared that they would overshoot the middle and fall into strange teachings; so he wished to go back and cut them to shape. Kong Anguo: they do not know how to cut it — 'I must go back and cut it for them'. Variant: He Yan's text ends 裁之也.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
伯夷、叔齊不念舊惡，
怨是用希。」

morph.gloss: Boyi — elder son of the lord of Guzhu

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Boyi and Shuqi did not keep old wrongs in mind;
resentment, because of this, was rare.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Boyi and Shuqi never dwelt on the wrongs men had done in the past, and so few bore them any grudge.”
sentences.n: 伯夷 Boyi and 叔齊 Shuqi were the two sons of the lord of Guzhu 孤竹 (Zhu Xi; He Yan's Kong Anguo), the Analects' model of purity; their story comes back in Book 7. 伯 and 叔 mark seniority among brothers. 惡 here is è, 'wrong, evil': 舊惡 'old wrongs', what others had done amiss in the past. 怨是用希 'resentment, by this, was rare': 是用 'by this' is like 是以, with the demonstrative object 是 before the word that governs it. 希 'rare'. Zhu Xi quotes Mencius on them: they would not stand at a bad man's court nor speak with a bad man, and standing beside a villager whose cap was askew they would walk off without a glance back, as if he would soil them — so strict that it seems no one could live with them; yet if the man they disliked could change, they stopped, so people did not much resent them. So in Zhu Xi the resentment is other people's; the words could also mean that they themselves seldom felt it. He quotes Master Cheng: not keeping old wrongs in mind is the breadth of the pure; and, who but the Master could have known the hearts of these two?

sentences.t:
子曰：「
孰謂微生髙直？
或乞醯焉，
乞諸其鄰而與之。」

morph.gloss: Weisheng Gao — a man of Lu
Gao (his personal name; 髙 = 高 'high')

sentences.i: The Master said: “Who says Weisheng Gao is an honest man? When someone came to him for vinegar, he went and got some from the people next door and handed it over as his own.”
sentences.n: 微生髙 Weisheng Gao (髙 is the edition's form of 高): surname Weisheng, personal name Gao, a man of Lu with a name for straightness (Zhu Xi; He Yan's Kong Anguo). 孰謂 'who says…?' is a rhetorical question. 醯 xī is vinegar (Zhu Xi: 呼西反，醋也). 焉 is the fused 於之 'of him', and 諸 the fused 之於 'it from'. 與 is yǔ, 'to give'. Zhu Xi: when the man came asking, Gao's house had none, so he begged some from a neighbour to give him; the Master mocks him for bending his own mind to please, taking credit for another's goods to buy goodwill — that cannot be called straight. He quotes Master Cheng: the twist was small, but the harm to straightness great; and Fan Zuyu: to call yes yes and no no, to say 'I have' when you have and 'I have not' when you have not — that is straightness; the sage judges a man by the least thing he takes or gives, and from that his conduct over a thousand teams of horses or ten thousand measures of grain can be known, so he judged by a small affair, to teach that one must be careful. Kong Anguo: begging from the neighbours to meet a request is a roundabout mind, not a straight man's.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
巧言、令色、足恭，
左丘明恥之，
丘亦恥之。
匿怨而友其人，
左丘明恥之，
丘亦恥之。」

morph.gloss: Zuo Qiuming — a worthy of Lu
Qiu: Confucius's own personal name (Kong Qiu 孔丘), used in speaking of himself

sentences.i: The Master said: “Smooth talk, a face put on to please, deference laid on too thick — Zuo Qiuming held these a disgrace, and so do I. To keep a grudge hidden and play the friend to the man — Zuo Qiuming held that a disgrace, and so do I.”
sentences.n: 巧言令色 is the pair of 1.3. 足 here is jù, 'to overdo' (Zhu Xi: 將樹反…過也), not zú 'enough'; 足恭 is courtesy carried to excess — He Yan's Kong Anguo: the look of one who bends and twists to please. 匿 is 'to hide'; 友 'friend' is used as a verb, 'to befriend'. 丘 Qiu is Confucius's own personal name: speaking of himself by it is the humble form. 左丘明 Zuo Qiuming: Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng that he was a famous man of old; Kong Anguo calls him a grandee of Lu; tradition makes him the author of the Zuo zhuan. Zhu Xi quotes Xie Liangzuo: these two things are more shameful than breaking through a wall to steal; that Zuo Qiuming was ashamed of them shows how he had nurtured himself; the Master's 'I, Qiu, too' is in the spirit of 'I privately compare myself to old Peng' (7.1), and a deep warning to learners to look into this and set their hearts on straightness.

sentences.t:
顔淵、季路侍。
子曰：「盍各言爾志？」

morph.gloss: Yan (a surname; 顔, the edition's form of 顏)

sentences.l:
Yan Yuan and Ji Lu were in attendance.
The Master said: “Why not each tell your aims?”
sentences.i: Yan Yuan and Ji Lu were attending on the Master. He said: “Why not each of you tell me where your aims lie?”
sentences.n: 顔淵 Yan Yuan is Yan Hui 顏回 of 2.9, courtesy name Ziyuan 子淵 (the edition prints 顔 here and 顏 two units on — two forms of one character). 季路 Ji Lu is another name for Zilu, Zhong You. 侍 shì is to attend on a superior, standing or sitting by. 盍 hé is 'why not?' (Zhu Xi: 盍音合，何不也), the fused form of 何不. 爾 'your'. 志 is what the heart is set on (2.4). Variant: He Yan's text reads 盍各曰爾志, 'say' for 'tell'.

sentences.t:
子路曰：「
願車馬、衣輕裘，
與朋友共，
敝之而無憾。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zilu said: “I wish that carriages and horses, and the light furs I wear,
I might share with friends,
and, though they were worn out, have no regret.”
sentences.i: Zilu said: “My wish is for my carriage and horses, and the light furs on my back, to be my friends' as much as mine — and if they wear them out, to feel no grudge.”
sentences.n: 願 is 'to wish'. 衣 is yì, the verb 'to wear' (Zhu Xi: 衣去聲…服之也), not yī 'clothes'; 裘 qiú is a fur robe, and light furs were costly. 共 is gòng, 'to share, to hold in common' — not the gǒng of 2.1. 敝 is 'worn out, spoiled' (Zhu Xi: 壞也); 憾 hàn is 'regret, rue' (Zhu Xi and He Yan's Kong Anguo: 恨也). 而 'and yet'. The transcription of our Ruan Yuan witness sets 輕 in round brackets, apparently marking it as a suspected later addition (the phrase 衣輕裘 occurs in Book 6, and may have drawn it in); Zhu Xi's text and He Yan's both have it, and so do we.

sentences.t:
顏淵曰：「
願無伐善，
無施勞。」

morph.gloss: Yuan (in 顏淵, from the courtesy name Ziyuan)

sentences.l:
Yan Yuan said: “I wish not to boast of what I do well,
not to make much of my services.”
sentences.i: Yan Yuan said: “My wish is never to boast of my abilities, and never to parade what I have accomplished.”
sentences.n: 無 negates the wish: 'not to…'. 伐 fá is 'to boast' (Zhu Xi: 誇也); 善 is what one is good at (Zhu Xi: 有能). 施, Zhu Xi says, also means puffing up, making much of (張大之意); 勞 is meritorious service (Zhu Xi: 有功), as in the Yijing's 勞而不伐 'toils and does not boast'. Zhu Xi records a second reading and allows it: 勞 is toilsome work, which one does not want for oneself and so does not wish to lay on others — 施 then is 'to impose'. That is the reading of He Yan's Kong Anguo (無以勞事置施於人 'not to put toilsome tasks on others'), who glosses the first half as 'not to proclaim one's own goodness'.

sentences.t:
子路曰：「願聞子之志。」
子曰：「
老者安之，
朋友信之，
少者懷之。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: Zilu said: “May we hear what you would wish for, Master?” The Master said: “That the old should have their ease, my friends my good faith, and the young my tender care.”
sentences.n: 子 here is 'you, Master', the disciples addressing him. 者 after 老 and 少 makes a topic: 'as for the old…'. 少 is shào, 'young', not shǎo 'few'. 之 'them' in each clause. Zhu Xi: the old I would nourish with ease, friends I would deal with in good faith, the young I would embrace with kindness; he records another reading which he also allows: 'the old are at ease with me, friends trust me, the young turn to me'. He quotes Master Cheng at length: the Master is at rest in humaneness, Yan Yuan does not depart from it, Zilu seeks it; all three wishes share things with others, differing only in size; Zilu, bold for what is right, could not be held by power or gain, and comes next to the man who would bathe in the Yi (Book 11); Yan Hui did not keep himself to himself, so did not boast, and knew he was one with others, so did not parade his toil — a large aim, yet still something willed; the Master is like the making-power of Heaven and Earth, which gives each thing its share and does not toil. And Cheng ends: in reading the Analects one must not only grasp the words but learn to recognize the bearing of sages and worthies.

sentences.t:
子曰：「巳矣乎！
吾未見能見其過
而内自訟者也。」

morph.gloss: finished (巳, the edition's form of 已)
inwardly (内, the edition's form of 內)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “It is finished!
I have not yet seen one who can see his own faults
and inwardly bring himself to trial.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “There is no hope of it. I have never come across anyone who sees his own faults and then arraigns himself in his own heart.”
sentences.n: 巳 is printed so here (He Yan's text uses 巳 for 已 throughout, and the Siku copy has 巳矣乎 in Zhu Xi's comment too); it is the word 已 yǐ, 'to stop, be over', and we keep the glyph. 已矣乎 'it is over!' — Zhu Xi: a sigh for fear of never seeing such a man after all. 訟 sòng is to bring a suit, to accuse (He Yan's Bao Xian: 責也 'to reproach'); 内自訟 Zhu Xi: the mouth says nothing, but the heart blames itself. 能見其過而内自訟者 is one long noun phrase closed by 者, 'one who can…'. Zhu Xi: few men who err know it themselves, fewer still can accuse themselves inwardly when they know; one who can will repent deeply and is sure to change. The Master sighs for fear he will never see it — a deep warning to learners.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
十室之邑，
必有忠信如丘者焉，
不如丘之好學也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “A town of ten households
is sure to have someone as wholehearted and true to his word as Qiu,
but not as fond of learning as Qiu.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Even a village of ten households is sure to hold someone as wholehearted and as good as his word as I am — but not one who loves learning as I do.”
sentences.n: 十室之邑 'a town of ten households', the smallest of places (Zhu Xi: 小邑). 丘 Qiu, again the Master speaking of himself by name. 焉 Zhu Xi reads as the closing particle of the first clause (焉如字屬上句 'belongs to the sentence above'), 'there is in it'; he is setting aside a reading that takes it as 'how?' opening the next clause: 'how could they not be as fond of learning as Qiu?'. 之 between 丘 and 好學 makes 'Qiu's loving learning'; 好 is hào (Zhu Xi: 去聲). Zhu Xi: to be wholehearted and true like a sage is a fine native endowment; the Master was born knowing and yet never stopped loving learning, and says this to spur others on — a fine endowment is easy to come by, the perfect Way hard to hear; learn to the utmost and you can become a sage; do not learn, and you stay a mere villager. Variant: He Yan's text ends 好學者也, 'one as fond of learning as Qiu'. Book 5 ends here, and with it the third juan of Zhu Xi's commentary.
